title: Elements and compounds
competency: Differentiate elements and compounds, and classify elements as metals and non-metals.

keywords.def: A pure substance that cannot be broken down into simpler substances by ordinary chemical means.
The smallest particle of an element.
An element that is shiny, conducts heat and electricity, and is malleable and ductile.
An element without metallic properties: dull and a poor conductor.
Can be drawn into thin wire.
A pure substance made of more than one type of atom bonded together.
A compound formed from two different elements, like sodium chloride.

en.text: An element is a pure substance that cannot be broken down into simpler substances by ordinary chemical means. It has only one kind of atom. 118 elements are known; 92 occur naturally. Metals like gold, iron and copper are shiny, conduct heat and electricity, and are malleable and ductile. Non-metals like carbon, oxygen and sulfur are dull and poor conductors.

screens.title: Why copper?
screens.ask: Electric wires are made of copper, not sulfur. Why?
screens.after:
Copper is a metal. Metals are good conductors of electricity.
Copper is also ductile: it can be drawn into thin wire.
Sulfur is a non-metal. It does not conduct, and it is a solid, not a liquid.

screens.title: 2.3.2 Elements
paras: An element is a pure substance that cannot be broken down by ordinary chemical means.
It has only one kind of particle, the atom.
At present 118 elements are known. 92 occur naturally on Earth.
Elements are divided into metals and non-metals.

screens.title: Metals
paras: Examples: gold, iron, silver, copper, aluminium, sodium, lead.
They are shiny (lustrous).
They are good conductors of heat and electricity.
Most have high density and high melting points.
They are malleable and ductile.
They are solid at room temperature, except mercury, a liquid.

screens.title: Non-metals
paras: Examples: carbon, oxygen, sulfur, fluorine, phosphorus.
They are dull and do not conduct heat or electricity.
They have low melting and boiling points.
Bromine is a liquid at room temperature.

screens.title: Table 2.3 Metals and non-metals
table: Solid at room temperature, except mercury
Exist as solids, liquids and gases
Very hard, except sodium and potassium

screens.title: Key words
defs: A pure substance that cannot be broken down into simpler substances by ordinary chemical means.
The smallest particle of an element.
An element that is shiny, conducts heat and electricity, and is malleable and ductile.
An element without metallic properties: dull and a poor conductor.
Can be drawn into thin wire.

screens.text: Which element is a metal that is liquid at room temperature?
screens.why:
Metals are solid at room temperature, except mercury.
So mercury is the liquid metal.
Bromine is also a liquid, but it is a non-metal.
Sodium and iron are solid metals.

items: Gold is shiny and malleable: a metal.
Sulfur is a dull yellow solid that does not conduct: a non-metal.
Copper conducts electricity well: a metal.
Oxygen is a gas and a poor conductor: a non-metal.
Aluminium is shiny and conducts: a metal.
screens.why:
Step 1: is it shiny and a good conductor? Then it is a metal.
Gold, copper and aluminium are metals.
Step 2: is it dull, or a gas, and a poor conductor? Then it is a non-metal.
Sulfur, oxygen and carbon are non-metals.
screens.clue: Is it shiny and a good conductor?
screens.text: Sort each element: is it a metal or a non-metal?
Identify the type of element: Substance Y is a hard, shiny solid that conducts heat and electricity well. Y is likely a …
screens.why:
List Y's properties: hard, shiny, solid, good conductor.
Table 2.3: these are all properties of metals.
A non-metal is dull and a poor conductor, so it is not a non-metal.
Y is a metal.

screens.ask: Name the property: a metal that can be hammered into thin sheets is called ___.
screens.why:
Hammered into sheets → malleable.
Drawn into thin wire → ductile.
So the word is malleable.

screens.text: Which non-metal is essential for our life, because we breathe it?
screens.why:
We breathe in air, which contains oxygen.
Our bodies use oxygen to release energy from food.
Oxygen is a non-metal (a gas).
Sulfur and fluorine are non-metals we do not breathe. Iron is a metal.
screens.clue: Which non-metal is in the air we breathe?

en.text: A compound is a pure substance made of more than one type of atom bonded together. It can be broken into its elements only by chemical means. Water breaks into hydrogen and oxygen with electricity. Sodium chloride is made of sodium and chlorine. A compound's properties differ from those of its elements.

screens.title: Iron + sulfur
screens.ask: Iron filings are mixed with sulfur. A magnet still pulls the iron out. After strong heating, the magnet no longer does. What happened?
opts: A new substance, a compound, formed
screens.after:
Before heating, iron and sulfur are only mixed, so the magnet pulls out the iron.
Heating joins them chemically into iron sulfide.
Iron sulfide is a new substance, a compound. It is not magnetic.
screens.best: A new substance, a compound, formed

screens.title: Compounds
paras: A compound is a pure substance made of more than one type of atom bonded together.
It can be broken into two or more elements by chemical means.
Electric current breaks water into hydrogen and oxygen.
Sodium chloride forms from sodium and chlorine.
A compound of two different elements is a binary compound.

screens.title: What distinguishes an element from a compound?
paras: A compound's properties are different from those of its elements.
In a compound the elements are chemically, not physically, combined.

screens.title: Experiment 2.2 Distinguishing compounds and mixtures
steps: Part I: mix 7 g iron powder with 4 g sulfur powder. The mixture is grey with yellow and black grains.
A magnet pulls the iron out. A mixture can be separated physically.
Part II (teacher demonstration, ventilated room): heat 2 g of mixture until it glows orange.
The glow spreads through the mixture by itself.
The product, iron(II) sulfide, is a black solid. A magnet does not pick it up.
A new substance with new properties formed: a compound.

screens.title: Element or compound? Tap each part.
sets: One kind of atom only. Cannot be broken down by ordinary chemical means. Examples: iron, gold, hydrogen.
More than one kind of atom, chemically joined. Split into elements only by chemical means. Examples: water, table salt.
overlaps: Both are pure substances. Neither can be separated by physical means like a magnet or a sieve.

screens.title: Key words
defs: A pure substance made of more than one type of atom bonded together.
A compound formed from two different elements, like sodium chloride.

screens.text: How can water be broken into hydrogen and oxygen?
screens.why:
Water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen.
A compound is split into its elements only by chemical means.
Passing an electric current through water does this.
Filtering, a magnet and sieving are physical methods: they cannot split a compound.
screens.clue: Physical methods cannot split a compound.

items: One kind of atom: iron atoms only.
Hydrogen and oxygen joined: a compound.
One kind of atom: gold atoms only.
Sodium and chlorine joined: a compound.
One kind of atom: hydrogen atoms only.
Carbon and oxygen joined: a compound.
screens.why:
Ask: how many kinds of atom does it have?
One kind → element: iron, gold, hydrogen.
Two or more kinds joined → compound: water (H + O), table salt (Na + Cl), carbon dioxide (C + O).
screens.clue: Is it made of one kind of atom?
screens.text: Sort each substance: is it an element or a compound?
True or false? Sodium chloride (table salt) has the same properties as sodium and chlorine.
screens.why:
Sodium is a soft metal. Chlorine is a poisonous gas.
Joined, they form sodium chloride: table salt, which we eat.
A compound's properties differ from those of its elements.
So the statement is false.
screens.clue: Do we eat chlorine gas? We eat table salt.

screens.text: Mixture or compound? Magnesium filings and sulfur are put in a beaker, then heated so they react to form magnesium sulfide. What is it before and after?
screens.why:
Before heating: magnesium and sulfur are only placed together. They are not joined: a mixture.
On heating they react chemically.
Magnesium sulfide is a new substance with new properties: a compound.
So: mixture before, compound after (like iron and sulfur in Experiment 2.2).

items.text: Experiment 2.2 Part I: what do you observe as you bring the magnet close to the iron–sulfur mixture?
opts: The iron filings stick to the magnet; the sulfur stays
items.ans: The iron filings stick to the magnet; the sulfur stays
items.why:
Iron is magnetic. Sulfur is not.
In a mixture, each substance keeps its own properties.
So the iron filings stick to the magnet and the sulfur stays behind.

items.text: Experiment 2.2 Part I: what do you see when you look at the mixture under a magnifying glass?
opts: Separate grains of grey iron and yellow sulfur
items.ans: Separate grains of grey iron and yellow sulfur
items.why:
In Part I nothing has been heated, so it is still a mixture.
In a mixture the particles are not joined.
So you see separate grey iron grains and yellow sulfur grains.
The black substance forms only after heating in Part II.
items.clue: Is it still a mixture in Part I?

items.text: Experiment 2.2 Part II: after heating, the black product is not attracted by a magnet. Why?
opts: A new compound, iron(II) sulfide, formed
items.ans: A new compound, iron(II) sulfide, formed
items.why:
Heating made iron and sulfur react chemically.
They formed iron(II) sulfide, a new compound.
A compound has properties different from its elements.
Iron sulfide is not magnetic, so the magnet does not pick it up.

test.text: Which of these substances is an element?
test.why:
An element has only one kind of atom.
Iron has only iron atoms: an element.
Water (H + O), table salt (Na + Cl) and sugar (C, H, O) each have more than one kind: compounds.

test.text: True or false? Metals are good conductors of heat and electricity.
test.why:
Table 2.3: metals conduct heat and electricity well.
That is why pots and electric wires are made of metal.
So the statement is true.

test.text: Which of these elements is not a metal?
test.why:
Iron, copper and sodium are metals: they conduct and are shiny when cut.
Sulfur is dull, brittle and does not conduct.
So sulfur is the non-metal.

test.text: How can a compound be broken into its elements? By …
test.why:
In a compound the elements are chemically joined.
Only a chemical method can break these bonds.
Example: an electric current splits water into hydrogen and oxygen.
A magnet and a sieve are physical means: they cannot split a compound.

test.text: What does ductility mean? Ductility means a metal can be …
test.why:
Ductile → can be drawn into thin wire (like copper wire).
Malleable → can be hammered into sheets (like iron roof sheets).
Do not mix up the two words.
So ductility means drawn into thin wire.

notes.text: Experiment 2.2 Part II is a teacher demonstration. Heating sulfur can give off toxic sulfur dioxide: do it in a ventilated room or fume cupboard, with eye protection.
Table 2.3 says non-metals are dull "except iodine"; graphite (carbon) is also shiny and conducts. The lesson does not say "only iodine".
